name: Ashpile Crawler's Layered Survival Rig
description: A full-body survival stack built over years of necessity. Base layer is a long-sleeve thermal compression shirt in faded ash-gray, the fabric pilled and thin at the elbows but still holding heat — the brand tag is gone, replaced with a strip of self-repair tape bearing a handwritten size in permanent marker. Over that sits a heavily patched canvas work shirt in stained olive, every pocket reinforced with riveted nylon corners, the left sleeve rolled up to expose a chrome forearm prosthetic with a makeshift rubber gasket duct-taped at the elbow joint to keep acid rain from seeping into the socket. Cargo trousers in rust-brown ripstop hang low on the hips, cinched with a belt fashioned from a strip of industrial conveyor rubber punched with a hand-drill, fitted with a salvaged hex-bolt buckle. The right thigh has a drop-leg utility pouch in cracked black nylon, stuffed visibly full. Boots are resoled so many times the sole is a patchwork of three different rubber compounds, the uppers wrapped at the ankles in waterproof seam-seal tape over cracked leather. A balaclava in mottled gray sits tucked at the collar, ready to be pulled up. Finishing the look is a salvaged construction worker's hi-viz vest worn as an outer shell, the reflective strips long since peeled off and replaced with acid-resistant patch panels in dull orange — practical not decorative.
functionality: Full-body acid rain resistance via layered coverage and seam-sealed boots. Drop-leg pouch for survival gear. Chrome-arm gasket prevents socket corrosion. Balaclava for respiratory protection. Multiple reinforced cargo pockets. Construction vest adds visibility in low-light industrial zones.
what_it_says: This person has been surviving the Shelf for a long time — not scraping by on luck but on accumulated practical knowledge. Every modification is deliberate. The chrome arm is older, maintained by hand, not serviced by a clinic. They are not looking for help and are not waiting to be noticed.
worn_by: chrome-arm workers priced out of prosthetic clinics
former factory workers displaced by automation
manufacturer: Self-assembled from salvage, construction surplus, and street market scraps
story_hooks: The hex-bolt buckle on the belt is stamped with a corponation serial number — it came from a piece of equipment that was officially destroyed in an industrial accident that killed eleven people. The wearer knows what it is.

The acid-resistant panels on the vest are a slightly different orange than standard construction issue — they're cut from a hazmat suit used by a specific cleanup crew. A TESSERA BioOps investigator notices.

The self-repair tape on the chrome arm's gasket is starting to fail. One bad rain is going to corrode the elbow joint. The wearer has twelve hours to find a replacement seal or lose the arm's range of motion permanently.

physical_description.visual_profile: A weathered, functional survival silhouette telling a story of years on the street. Layered and deliberately over-equipped, with visible wear patterns and jury-rigged repairs that create a complex visual texture. The figure appears compact and ready for immediate action, with asymmetrical details (rolled sleeve, drop-leg pouch) suggesting someone who lives in their clothes.
physical_description.fit: Deliberately loose and utilitarian — the compression base layer fits close for heat retention, but the work shirt and cargo trousers hang roomily to allow for movement and additional gear. The hi-viz vest drapes as an outer shell without constraint. Everything is sized for function over form.
physical_description.primary_material: Thermal compression blend (base, synthetic/cotton mix, heavily worn), heavy canvas (work shirt), ripstop cotton-nylon blend (trousers), salvaged industrial materials (belt, tape seals), cracked leather and resoled rubber (boots), nylon (utility pouch and patches), hi-viz poly-cotton (outer vest)
physical_description.texture: Heavily textured with intentional roughness — pilled fabric on the base layer, stained and creased canvas, visible stitching and rivet work, duct-taped seams, waterproof tape overlays creating ridged surfaces, worn leather with visible cracks, mismatched rubber sole compounds with uneven wear
physical_description.color_scheme: Dominant palette of ash-gray, muted olive, rust-brown, and cracked charcoal black, with dull orange acid-resistant patches replacing the original hi-viz reflective strips. Accented by silver-chrome prosthetic limb and the metallic hex-bolt buckle. No bright colors — everything aged and desaturated.
physical_description.closures: Functional and varied — friction-fit compression base, canvas work shirt appears button-front (buttons likely replaced or missing), cargo trousers with likely a zipper fly and belt closure via the salvaged hex-bolt buckle, multiple riveted nylon reinforcements on pockets, waterproof tape seals on boots, duct tape securing the prosthetic gasket
distinctive_features: Exposed chrome forearm prosthetic with makeshift rubber gasket duct-taped at elbow joint
Heavily riveted and reinforced cargo pockets with visible nylon corner patches
Asymmetrical left sleeve rolled to expose augmentation
Drop-leg utility pouch in cracked nylon, visibly overstuffed with unidentified gear
Industrial conveyor rubber belt with hand-drilled holes and salvaged hex-bolt buckle
Balaclava tucked at collar, ready for deployment
Patched hi-viz vest with dull orange acid-resistant panels replacing reflective strips
Boots with resoled soles showing three different rubber compounds
Waterproof seam-seal tape wrapped around ankle joints
Handwritten size marker on self-repair tape replacing original brand tag
Asymmetrical weathering suggesting constant use and environmental exposure
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 5 sub-grade salvage aesthetic — every piece is either second-hand, repurposed from industrial surplus, or self-modified from street market scraps. No new manufactured garments. The outfit screams survival necessity over consumer choice.
physical_description.cultural_context: Street survivor, likely someone who works in the ungoverned ashpiles or acid-rain zones of the GLMZ. The augmentation and jury-rigged repairs suggest someone who has invested in keeping themselves functional through self-maintenance rather than corporate repair shops. This is the clothing of someone who cannot afford to fail — every pocket, every seal, every patch is there because they've needed it before.
physical_description.condition_typical: Perpetually weathered and in active use. Worn through at stress points (elbows, seat, knees), visibly stained with industrial grime, patches and repairs in various states of degradation, duct tape needing regular replacement, boot soles wearing unevenly, fabric pilling and thinning but still functional. This outfit improves with wear because every new tear gets addressed with another repair.
